text.p: There are fans and fanatics. And then there are Greek basketball supporters.
Any neutral in Rome for the Final Four where Olympiakos meet Barcelona for the European club title on Thursday needs at the very least state-of-the-art ear-plugs.
NBA deputy commissioner, Russ Granik, experiencing the phenomenon for the first time at Tuesday's semifinals, can testify.

Granik commented: "We have a lot of NBA teams that think they have loud fans and loud arenas and some of you may know we have issues from time to time at our arenas with people complaining that the noise level is too high.
"But there is nothing that I've seen at NBA or NCAA games that I've attended in my life time that are anything to compare with the level we experienced last night."
Like all the top Greek clubs, Olympiakos carry a huge, fervent following.

The ritual begins about an hour before the game is due to start. Festooned in the club colours, the fans unfurl their massive flags (including one from their London section) and drape them over the balconies.

Then the chanting and the singing begin. Then the musical instruments and the rhythmic clapping, fans with arms aloft in unison forming a great sea of red and white covering half the 10,800-seater Palaeur stadium.
It hardly seems possible for the noise, magnified as it is by the indoor arena, to get any louder, yet it does. The whole scenario almost seems orchestrated yet it cannot be.
When Olympiakos attack it is to the accompaniment of massive roars, cheers, singing and waving of arms. When they score there is the kind of cheer that greets a goal at a major cup final.
When the opposition have the ball they are met by a wall of booing and whistling, so shrill in its intensity as to be hardly sufferable.
The noise is constant. Only halftime brings a respite and then it is back to the drama.
When the opposing fans cheer it is quickly countered and drowned. Ljubljana supporters were outnumbered 10-1 but Barcelona will be more of a contest on Thursday.
"I had only heard about this type of fan loyalty," said Granik. "It's something you have to see and something you have to hear for yourselves."
With such passionate intensity, a casual observer might be forgiven for wondering about the Greek suicide rate were Olympiakos, beaten finalists in 1994 and 1995, to fail again on Thursday.
On occasions, despair has spilled over and violence is not unknown to Greek basketball.

However, FIBA, the international organisation, has entrusted the 1998 world championships to Athens and Granik's verdict on Tuesday night, featuring two hard-fought semis and the massed ranks of the Olympiakos faithful, was that it had been "extremely exciting".

And Warren Brown, USA Basketball chief executive, thought it might have benefitted potential U.S.national squad players to savour Tuesday's "wonderful atmosphere" as a prelude to what can be expected in Greece next year.
"We are looking forward to selecting a team that will go to Athens and participate," he said.
